Archival Silence and the Digital Record

Submitted to the Harrington Trust, Documentary Heritage Program
(fabricated fixture document — every person, work, and finding is invented)

The premise that digitization guarantees preservation has been
challenged repeatedly (Whitfield 2020). Format obsolescence outpaces
migration budgets in most public archives (Reyes and Calloway 2018).
Whitfield (2020) describes the resulting losses as "a slow fire in the
server room, consuming collections nobody has opened recently." One
influential account attributes the gap to donor preference for visible
acquisitions (Bellweather 2017).

As Nakamura (2019a) shows, community archives fill part of the gap,
though their holdings skew heavily toward the recent past
(Nakamura 2019b). The proposed survey extends that work to
born-digital municipal records.

References

Nakamura, Keiko. 2019a. "Community Archives and the Recent Past."
Archival Practice 31 (2): 88-107. https://doi.org/10.2345/ap.2019.312

Nakamura, Keiko. 2019b. Memory Without Institutions. Portland:
Cascadia University Press.

Reyes, Marisol, and Duncan Calloway. 2018. "Migration Debt in Public
Archives." Journal of Digital Preservation 11 (1): 3-29.

Whitfield, Amara. 2020. The Slow Fire: Loss in Born-Digital
Collections. Chicago: Imagined Press.
